# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–23 (Complete – Updated 167)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of sixth year, afternoon/evening of Sunday** (Chapter 23). Rawdon discovered Rebecca with Steyne, confronted them, visited Pitt to arrange guardianship of little Rawdon, and arranged duel with Steyne. Duel now formally initiated; seconds communicating. Amelia continues evening vigils at Russell Square. Little Rawdon at school.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opened "summer of sixth year"; Chapter 23 opens "autumn of sixth year." Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph.
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton); Queen's Crawley; rural Fenmere (minor).

## The Catastrophic Discovery and Immediate Aftermath (Chapters 22–23)

**Rawdon's Return Home and Confrontation (Chapter 22–23)**: Found drawing-room blazing with light at nine o'clock. Found Steyne bowing to kiss Rebecca's hand; Rebecca sat in brilliant toilette, arms sparkling with bracelets given by Steyne. Rawdon seized Steyne by neckcloth, struck him twice over face with open hand, flung him bleeding to ground. Steyne wore scar to dying day.

**Jewel and Financial Discovery (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon flung open boxes and wardrobes, found desk Amelia had given Rebecca containing papers, love-letters, trinkets, and pocket-book with bank-notes. **CRITICAL DISCOVERY**: Bank-notes including fresh note for **one thousand pounds from Lord Steyne**—evidence of extensive financial support constituting payment for sexual favors.

**Rebecca's Immediate Aftermath (Chapter 23)**: Remained alone for hours, certain "he would never come back. He was gone forever." Experienced suicidal ideation: considered laudanum. French maid (accomplice, in Steyne's pay) persuaded her to rest on bed with kindness. Maid gathered trinkets from floor. By afternoon, Rebecca awakened from stupor when chapel bells rang for afternoon service. Rang for maid repeatedly, pulled down bell-rope in desperation, screamed from landing with hair loose.

**Rebecca's Revelation of Heritage (Chapter 23)**: Rebecca claimed innocence before God. Rawdon screamed: "You're as innocent as your mother, the ballet-girl, and your husband the bully." **REVELATION**: Rebecca's mother was a ballet-girl; her father (characterized by Rawdon) was a bully.

## Rawdon's Actions and Duel Arrangements (Chapter 23)

**Morning Meeting with Pitt (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon arrived at Great Gaunt Street in evening costume worn two days, blood-shot eyed, tumbled clothes. Pitt appeared fresh and neat, initially thought Rawdon intoxicated. Pitt refused financial help: "Even the hundred pounds that Jane took you last night were promised to my lawyer to-morrow morning."

**Rawdon's Confession and Request (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon spoke in husky voice: "It's the boy. I want you to promise me that you will take charge of him when I'm gone." Revealed full circumstances of financial manipulation and Rebecca's infidelity. Pitt instantly guessed Rawdon intended to duel Steyne. Rawdon asked: "I must leave him to you and Jane, Pitt--only it will be a comfort to me if you will promise me to be his friend."

**Financial Settlement (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon drew pocket-book found in Becky's desk: "Here's six hundred--I want you to give the money to Briggs, who lent it to us--and who was kind to the boy--and I've always felt ashamed of having taken the poor old woman's money. And here's some more--I've only kept back a few pounds--which Becky may as well have." Thousand-pound note fell out.

**Challenge to Steyne (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon knocked at Gaunt House, handed card to purple Silenus porter: "Colonel Crawley would be all day after one o'clock at the Regent Club in St. James's Street--not at home." Proceeded to Knightsbridge Barracks.

**Meeting with Captain Macmurdo (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon reached Knightsbridge on Sunday morning and found Captain Macmurdo at home in barracks. Macmurdo (age nearly fifty, twenty-four years in regiment, best shots and riders in England, Rawdon's former rival, Waterloo veteran) was reading Bell's Life. Macmurdo knew duel arrangements perfectly—"common refuge of gentlemen in trouble."

**Macmurdo's Role as Second (Chapter 23)**: Composed letter to Steyne on behalf of Colonel Rawdon Crawley requesting appointment of friend to arrange meeting "with as little delay as possible." Letter delivered via Macmurdo's servant to Regent Club.

**Rawdon's Emotional Revelation (Chapter 23)**: Covered face with hands, overcome: "You don't know how fond I was of that one...I followed her like a footman. I gave up everything I had to her. I'm a beggar because I would marry her. By Jove, sir, I've pawned my own watch in order to get her anything she fancied; and she--she's been making a purse for herself all the time, and grudged me a hundred pound to get me out of quod." Showed Macmurdo thousand-pound note as evidence of Rebecca's guilt and selfishness.

**Rawdon's Paternal Concern (Chapter 23)**: "He's a regular trump, that boy...I say, Mac, if anything goes wrong--if I drop--I should like you to--to go and see him, you know, and say that I was very fond of him...give him these gold sleeve-buttons: it's all I've got." Covered face with black hands, tears rolled.

**Preparation for Duel (Chapter 23)**: Macmurdo ordered breakfast with cheerful voice—"devilled kidneys and a herring." Offered Rawdon clean clothes from own wardrobe ("we were always pretty much of a size, Rawdon, my boy"). Rawdon dressed while Macmurdo read Bell's Life. Macmurdo performed his own toilette with particular care: waxed mustachios into brilliant polish, put on tight cravat and buff waistcoat. Young officers at mess-room breakfast complimented Mac on appearance, joked he was "going to be married that Sunday"—oblique reference to duel protocol. At breakfast post-duel-preparation: Young Lord Varinas smoking Meerschaum pipe; Captain Hugues with cigar; Tandyman with bull-terrier tossing for shillings against Captain Deuceace. Mac and Rawdon joined gaily in conversation without hint of business occupying their minds. Both maintained composure; "Feasting, drinking, ribaldry, laughter, go on alongside of all sorts of other occupations in Vanity Fair." As church crowds poured out, Rawdon and Macmurdo walked off to Regent Club on St. James's Street.

## The Dissolution of Curzon Street Household (Chapter 23)

**Mademoiselle Fifine's Abandonment and Theft (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon's servant reported: "There's a regular shinty in the house, and everything at sixes and sevens. The landlord's come in and took possession." When Rebecca rang for maid Mademoiselle Fifine in afternoon, maid did not appear.

**Fifine's Escape**: Fifine had quit premises hours before "on French leave." After picking up trinkets from drawing-room, Fifine packed her own boxes in her apartment, called cab herself, brought down trunks single-handed without aid from other servants (who hated her), and departed Curzon Street without saying goodbye to anyone. "The game, in her opinion, was over in that little domestic establishment."

**Fifine's Thefts**: Beyond her own property, Fifine secured items belonging to Rebecca: four richly gilt Louis Quatorze candlesticks, six gilt albums, keepsakes, Books of Beauty, gold enamelled snuff-box once belonging to Madame du Barri, sweetest little inkstand and mother-of-pearl blotting book (which Becky used for charming pink notes), and all silver laid on table for small entertainment Rawdon had interrupted. She left behind: plated ware, fire irons, chimney-glasses, and rosewood cottage piano (too cumbrous).

**Fifine's Later Life (Chapter 23)**: Subsequently kept milliner's shop in Rue du Helder, Paris, under name Madame de Saint-Amaranthe, living "with great credit" and enjoying patronage of Lord Steyne. Always spoke of England "as of the most treacherous country in the world" and claimed she had been "affreusement volé by natives of that island." "May she flourish as she deserves--she appears no more in our quarter of Vanity Fair."

**Household Mutiny (Chapter 23)**: When Rebecca, in white cashmere dressing-gown, entered drawing-room after ringing unanswered, found: cook with blackened face seated on chintz sofa beside Mrs. Raggles, administering Maraschino; page with sugar-loaf buttons putting fingers in cream dish; footman talking to Raggles (face full of perplexity and woe); servants entirely indifferent to Rebecca's calls. None obeyed though door was open and Becky had screamed multiple times.

**Cook's Rebellion (Chapter 23)**: Cook defiantly drank Maraschino, declaring: "YOUR sofy, indeed! I'm a settin' on Mrs. Raggles's sofy...which they bought with honest money...And I'm thinkin' if I set here until I'm paid my wages, I shall set a precious long time...set I will, too--ha! ha!" Servants burst into laughter; Raggles maintained "most melancholy countenance" and did not join.

**Trotter's Accusation (Chapter 23)**: Footman Trotter, flushed and inebriated, announced: "He ain't a coming back...He sent for his things, and I wouldn't let 'em go, although Mr. Raggles would; and I don't b'lieve he's no more a Colonel than I am. He's hoff, and I suppose you're a goin' after him. You're no better than swindlers, both on you. Don't be a bullyin' ME. I won't stand it. Pay us our selleries, I say." Simpson the page prevented further outrage but Trotter's sentiment unchallenged.

**Raggles's Lament (Chapter 23 – New Excerpt 1384)**: Raggles wept in lamentation: "I never thought to live to see this year day: I've known the Crawley family ever since I was born. I lived butler with Miss Crawley for thirty years; and I little thought one of that family was a goin' to ruing me--yes, ruing me." Enumerated griefs truthfully: Becky and Rawdon had ruined him. Bills coming due next week with no means to meet them. Would be sold up and turned out of shop and house because he had trusted to the Crawley family. He was owed milk and butter bill of two hundred pounds. All statements true. His tears and lamentations made Becky more peevish than ever.

## Rebecca's Final Attempt at Reconciliation (Chapter 23 – New Excerpts 1386–1390)

**Rebecca's Audacious Lie (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1386)**: When servants demanded payment, Rebecca claimed bitter bewilderment: "You all seem to be against me. What do you want? I can't pay you on Sunday. Come back to-morrow and I'll pay you everything. I thought Colonel Crawley had settled with you. He will to-morrow. I declare to you upon my honour that he left home this morning with fifteen hundred pounds in his pocket-book. He has left me nothing. Apply to him." **CRITICAL LIE**: Rawdon actually left with considerably less; Rebecca falsely claimed he possessed fifteen hundred pounds. "Give me a bonnet and shawl and let me go out and find him. There was a difference between us this morning. You all seem to know it. I promise you upon my word that you shall all be paid. He has got a good appointment. Let me go out and find him."

**Rebecca's Discovery of Fifine's Departure (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1387)**: Rebecca's audacious statement caused Raggles and others present to look at one another with wild surprise. She went upstairs and dressed herself without aid of French maid. Went into Rawdon's room and found trunk and bag packed ready for removal with pencil direction to give when called for. Went into Frenchwoman's garret; everything clean and all drawers emptied. Realized woman had fled. "Good Heavens! was ever such ill luck as mine? to be so near, and to lose all. Is it all too late?" Resolved: "No; there was one chance more."

**Rebecca's Appeal to Pitt (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1387–1388)**: At four o'clock, dressed and went away unmolested but alone. Walked swiftly down streets (had no money for carriage) and went directly to Sir Pitt Crawley's door in Great Gaunt Street. Lady Jane was at church; Becky was not sorry. Sir Pitt in his study with orders not to be disturbed; Becky slipped by sentinel in livery and was in his room before astonished Baronet laid down paper.

**Rebecca's False Account to Pitt (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1388)**: Rebecca told Sir Pitt: "It is true. Lord Steyne told me on Friday night, the night of that fatal ball. He has been promised an appointment any time these six months. Mr. Martyr, the Colonial Secretary, told him yesterday that it was made out. That unlucky arrest ensued; that horrible meeting. I was only guilty of too much devotedness to Rawdon's service. I have received Lord Steyne alone a hundred times before. I confess I had money of which Rawdon knew nothing. Don't you know how careless he is of it, and could I dare to confide it to him?" **CLAIM (UNVERIFIED)**: Rawdon promised an appointment by Colonial Secretary Martyr. Rebecca's account contained perfectly connected false story poured into ears of perplexed kinsman.

**Lady Jane's Intervention (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1388–1389)**: Lady Jane entered, trembling in every limb and turning quite pale. Her Ladyship had sent out maid directly after breakfast, who had communicated with Raggles and Rawdon Crawley's household, learning all of the story and a great deal more than they knew, plus many other stories besides. Lady Jane said: "I am surprised that woman has the audacity to enter this house. How dare Mrs. Crawley to enter the house of--of an honest family?"

**Lady Jane's Ultimatum (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1389)**: Lady Jane's clear voice thrilled; her heart beat violently as she spoke: "To be a wicked woman--a heartless mother, a false wife? She never loved her dear little boy, who used to fly here and tell me of her cruelty to him. She never came into a family but she strove to bring misery with her and to weaken the most sacred affections with her wicked flattery and falsehoods. She has deceived her husband, as she has deceived everybody; her soul is black with vanity, worldliness, and all sorts of crime. I tremble when I touch her. I keep my children out of her sight." Sir Pitt attempted interruption: "Lady Jane! this is really language--" Lady Jane continued, intrepidly: "I have been a true and faithful wife to you, Sir Pitt. I have kept my marriage vow as I made it to God and have been obedient and gentle as a wife should. But righteous obedience has its limits, and I declare that I will not bear that--that woman again under my roof; if she enters it, I and my children will leave it. She is not worthy to sit down with Christian people. You--you must choose, sir, between her and me." Lady Jane swept out of room, fluttering with her own audacity, leaving Rebecca and Sir Pitt astonished.

**Rebecca's Success with Pitt (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1390)**: Becky was not hurt; was pleased. "It was the diamond-clasp you gave me," she said to Sir Pitt, reaching him out her hand. Before she left him (Lady Jane watching from dressing-room window in upper story), Baronet had promised to go and seek out his brother and endeavour to bring about a reconciliation. So they went on talking about dancers, fights, drinking, demireps.

## Key Relationships and Character States

**Rawdon**: Complete moral regeneration. Transformed from spendthrift to responsible father. Prepared for death; entrusted son to Pitt and Jane; settled debts using Steyne's money; arranged duel as matter of honor. Emotional depth revealed: profound love for Rebecca now revealed as misplaced; genuine paternal affection for little Rawdon strong and genuine. Currently at Knightsbridge Barracks with Macmurdo, awaiting Steyne's response to challenge. Maintains composure and gaily participates in barracks breakfast conversation despite imminent danger.

**Rebecca**: Utterly ruined yet resourceful. Exposed as Steyne's paid mistress. Husband gone forever. Curzon Street household in chaos—landlord taken possession, servants drunk and mutinous, wages unpaid. Maid fled with valuable plunder. Now spreading false claims: Rawdon left with fifteen hundred pounds (lie); Rawdon promised Colonial appointment (UNVERIFIED CLAIM); insists she was innocent, merely devoted to Rawdon's service. Has successfully manipulated Pitt into promise of reconciliation. Facing scandal, but not yet acknowledging complete defeat.

**Steyne**: Exposed as financial corruptor and seducer. Scarred by Rawdon's assault; wore scar to dying day. Has received challenge via Macmurdo. Awaits formal duel arrangements. Continuing to support Fifine in Paris as Madame de Saint-Amaranthe.

**Pitt and Lady Jane**: Jane rescued Rawdon from spunging-house; entrusted with little Rawdon's guardianship should Rawdon die. Pitt refuses financial help; all money tied up in lawyer commitments (hundred pounds promised tomorrow). Promised six hundred pounds (from Steyne's money via Rawdon) for Briggs and little Rawdon's care. Pitt has promised to seek out Rawdon and attempt reconciliation at Rebecca's urging. Lady Jane firmly opposes any contact with Rebecca; made ultimatum to Pitt choosing between Rebecca and Lady Jane/children.

**Little Rawdon**: At school; being initiated into Latin Grammar. Happy and laughing in black gown and breeches. Will receive six hundred pounds and gold sleeve-buttons (Rawdon's gift) if Rawdon dies.

**Amelia**: Continued anguish. Separated from son; son indifferent to separation. Care-worn, sad, sleeps little, weeps and prays. Evening vigils at Russell Square.

**Captain Macmurdo**: Age nearly fifty, twenty-four years in regiment, veteran of Waterloo, best shots and riders in England, former rival of Rawdon. Conducting Rawdon's duel arrangements with care and professionalism. Has greatest regard from Royal Highness late Commander-in-Chief. Not exactly a lady's man; men asked him to dine at mistresses' houses rather than mothers' houses. Famous for good stories and choice ribaldry. Quite contented with his life; leads it in perfect good nature, simplicity, and modesty of demeanor.

**Briggs**: Lent money to Rawdon and Rebecca; kind to little Rawdon. Will receive six hundred pounds from Rawdon via Pitt.

**Mr. Raggles**: Landlord/shopkeeper. Lived butler with Miss Crawley for thirty years. Known Crawley family since birth. Ruined by trusting Rawdon and Rebecca; bills coming due next week; will be sold up and turned out of shop and house. Owed milk and butter bill of two hundred pounds. Weeping, sorrowful, maintaining melancholy countenance throughout household mutiny.

**Servants at Curzon Street**: Cook (blackened face, drunk on Maraschino); Simpson page (sugar-loaf buttons, young, affected by mistress's plight); Trotter footman (drunk, mutinous, accusing); others drinking and demanding unpaid wages.

**Mademoiselle Fifine**: French maid, accomplice to Rebecca's affair, in Steyne's pay. Has fled to Paris, opened milliner's shop as Madame de Saint-Amaranthe under Steyne's patronage. Stole four gilt candelabra, six albums, keepsakes, gold snuff-box, inkstand, blotting book, silver table service. "May she flourish as she deserves--she appears no more in our quarter of Vanity Fair."

**CRITICAL STATE**: Duel between Rawdon and Steyne formally initiated. Rawdon at Knightsbridge Barracks with Macmurdo, walking to Regent Club as church crowds pour out. Steyne has received challenge; response forthcoming "with as little delay as possible." Curzon Street household completely collapsed; Rebecca abandoned by servants, maid fled with plunder, landlord in possession. Rebecca has mounted final appeal to Pitt with false/unverified claims; partially successful. Rawdon's son's future secured; debts to be settled from Steyne's money. Duel imminent.
